name: Adikesava Perumal Temple, Thiruvattar
deity: Vishnu as Adikesava Perumal, reclining on the serpent Adishesha, with the Goddess Maragathavalli
period: A Divya Desam of Malai Nadu ringed by the Kothai and Parali rivers, sung by Nammalvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
summary: Where the Kothai and Parali rivers curve around a raised island, Vishnu reclines as Adikesava Perumal on the serpent Adishesha — a Malai Nadu Divya Desam sung by Nammalvar, kin in form to Padmanabha of Thiruvananthapuram.

sections.history: Thiruvattar — 'the place of the encircling river' — is one of the 108 Divya Desams, the abodes of Vishnu sung by the Alvars in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and is counted among the shrines of Malai Nadu, the Divya Desams of the Kerala country. Nammalvar sang its reclining lord. The temple's recorded history reaches back to an inscription of the Chola emperor Rajendra I on its bali stone, which names the deity as the god of Thiruvattar. In later centuries the rulers of Venad, forebears of the Travancore royal house, became its patrons: an inscription ascribes the single-stone mandapa to Veera Ravi Varma Kulasekhara, and in the late nineteenth century Moolam Thirunal Rama Varma of Travancore renewed the temple's flagstaff.
sections.architecture: The temple stands on raised ground with the rivers curving around it, its granite sanctum roofed in copper in the manner of the Kerala country. Before the sanctum is the Ottakkal Mandapam, the hall associated with a single great stone, whose building is recorded in an inscription of the Venad kings. The reclining image is around 22 feet long — so long that, as at Thiruvananthapuram, it is seen in portions through the three doorways of the sanctum: face, body and feet. One hand hangs gently down while the other is raised in blessing, an uncommon pose.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that the demons Kesan and Kesi rose to trouble the world, and that Vishnu overcame Kesi and lay down upon him, taking the name Adikesava. Tradition adds that Kesi's wife called on the rivers to sweep the place away, and that the lord raised the ground so that the waters could only flow around it like a garland — the encircling river that gives Thiruvattar its name. Devotees say the lord faces west, toward his kinsman Padmanabha at Thiruvananthapuram.
sections.festivals: The Brahmotsavam in the Tamil month of Aippasi (October–November) is the temple's great festival, with processions of the utsava deity. Vaikunta Ekadashi in Margazhi, the Saturdays of Purattasi and Onam are kept with devotion, and in Panguni (March–April) devotees gather for the evenings when the setting sun's rays are said to fall upon the reclining lord.
sections.experience: Come in the cool of the morning, when the rivers below the temple catch the light and the sanctum lamps are lit. Take time at the three doorways to see the reclining lord in turn, then rest in the Ottakkal Mandapam. Many pilgrims pair Thiruvattar with the Padmanabhaswamy temple at Thiruvananthapuram and with Thiruvanparisaram near Nagercoil, the other Malai Nadu shrines of this southern country.

visit.timings: Open daily with morning and evening darshan and a midday closure, following the temple's own schedule; festival days are crowded. Confirm current timings locally before you visit.
visit.dressCode: Traditional dress is expected: following the Kerala custom observed here, men may be asked to remove their shirts and enter in a dhoti, and women wear saree or other traditional dress; footwear is left outside. Follow posted rules and the guidance of temple staff.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted in and around the sanctum; follow posted rules and the guidance of temple staff.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvattar lies in Kalkulam taluk of Kanyakumari district, inland from Marthandam, and is reached by road from Marthandam, Kuzhithurai or Nagercoil. Kuzhithurai and Nagercoil have railway stations, and Thiruvananthapuram has the nearest airport.
